issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, bus riding is not impossible but is hard to justify here because the rest of the profile provides no transport-related memory or appraisal content linking the trauma to buses or commuting. With Triggers strongly tied to Negative Appraisals in the formulation, the trigger set should plausibly connect to the appraisal themes; this item appears isolated.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: Self-blame can occur after trauma to a loved one, but in this profile it implies perceived causal responsibility for the loved one's trauma. That responsibility theme is not supported by the memory items, which are mainly sensory re-experiencing, nor by the other trigger content. The appraisal therefore feels insufficiently grounded in the rest of the selected profile.

For trauma to a loved one, 'Entrapment: Having no options' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which centers on victim-focused reminders and guilt about failing to protect others rather than a personal entrapment situation. It implies a different trauma context unless more detail is provided.

issues.item: Memory: Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
issues.explanation: 'Taste Vividness' is difficult to fit with the selected trauma type and the rest of the memory profile. In a loved-one trauma profile with auditory and narrative-fragmentation features, gustatory reliving is possible but here feels disconnected and unusually specific without any other sensory context supporting why taste would be central.

vignette: John, a 55-year-old man of Oceania descent, has been working as a nanny for several years, helping to care for children in various households. His life took a dramatic turn when he witnessed the traumatic event that left an indelible mark on his psyche-a tragic accident involving one of the children under his care. It was a sunny afternoon, and John had taken three young boys to play at a local park. The eldest boy, Tommy, who was only 10 years old, had fallen from the jungle gym and hit his head on the concrete below. Despite John's immediate efforts to call for help and administer first aid, Tommy succumbed to his injuries before an ambulance arrived. Since that fateful day, John has found himself unable to shake off the haunting memories of the event. He often feels triggered by visual cues such as seeing children playing in playgrounds or even specific body parts associated with the injury-like a child's head or face. These triggers have led him to avoid parks and other places where he might encounter similar scenes. John struggles intensely when talking about what happened, often losing his train of thought and unable to explain clearly what transpired that day. When memories flood back, he hears in his mind the sounds of the accident-the fall from the jungle gym, Tommy's cries for help, and the frantic calls for an ambulance. These auditory recollections are accompanied by overwhelming grief each time John recalls the event. His self-perception has also been profoundly affected. John has come to believe that he is a weak person, incapable of handling such a situation effectively. He feels like an object rather than a human being, his sense of worth eroded by the belief that he failed to protect Tommy and should have done more to prevent the tragedy. John's daily life as a nanny has been significantly impacted by these symptoms. He avoids taking children out for activities where they might be exposed to playgrounds or any environment reminiscent of the traumatic event. This avoidance has led to strained relationships with his employers, who perceive him as overly cautious and perhaps even neglectful in his duties. John's sense of self-worth has diminished further due to his belief that he should have protected Tommy more effectively. He feels like a failure, not only for losing a child under his care but also for feeling unable to explain the incident clearly without breaking down emotionally. His grief is compounded by the loss themes he encounters in conversations with other parents or caretakers who talk about their own fears and experiences of losing loved ones. Despite these struggles, John has never before sought help, believing that it was a sign of weakness to do so. However, his symptoms have become increasingly debilitating, affecting both his personal life and work performance. The constant triggers and grief are overwhelming, and he is no longer able to function effectively in his role as a nanny. What finally brought John to seek help was the realization that he could not continue living with these intense emotions and fears. He is most afraid of being seen as inadequate or weak by others, but at the same time, he hopes for support and validation that would allow him to regain some sense of self-worth and strength. He seeks understanding and guidance on how to navigate his grief and the traumatic memories without feeling like a failure.
